newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia jobs rise masks underlying weakness.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia jobs rise masks underlying weakness.

text.p: Australian employment bounced back in October after a shock slide the month before, but the growth was still not enough to keep the unemployment rate from rising.

The data showed 25,500 new jobs were created, regaining some of the 34,100 loss recorded in September. However, a bigger rise in the number of people looking for work meant the unemployment rate ticked up to 8.8 percent from 8.7 percent, uncomfortably close to the politically sensitive 9.0 percent level.
"The jobs growth wasn't spectacular," said Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen. "It's just a sign the economy is still firing on three out of four cylinders."

As such, analysts reckoned the data supported the Reserve Bank's decision on Wednesday to lop 0.5 point off official interest rates to 6.5 percent and did not rule out the chance of another easing down the track.

"We're seeing around about 10-12,000 in growth in employment per month which is just barely enough to keep the new entrants to the labour force and population growth in check," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
"Therefore we see the unemployment rate stalled around this level, which politically is way too high. This will probably keep the speculation of another rate cut going," he said.

Akis Haralabopoulos, chief economist at GIO Australia, emphasised that employment was a lagging indicator on the economy and he saw good reason to expect domestic growth to accelerate next year and eventually lift jobs growth.
"If the global economy shapes up as we expect and the two rate cuts we've had begin to bite, then jobs will pick-up as 1997 progresses," he said.

"That's almost certainly the way the RBA sees it, which means the bank will sit on its hands until February or March before deciding if another easing is needed," he added, echoing a widespread sentiment among analysts.
The Australian government conceded the labour market was relatively weak, but was optimistic the 100 basis points of policy easing seen since July would eventually tell.
"Yesterday's interest rate reduction should provide a further boost to the labour market, though it may take some time for this to flow through," said Employment Minister Amanda Vanstone.
The October labour report was not without its bright spots - full-time employment for instance rose around 9,800.
But leading indicators such as the ANZ job advertisement series show few signs of an upturn on the horizon.

"With indicators such as retail sales showing economic activity remains at best sluggish, it is likely the unemployment rate will rise over the next few months and could reach 9.0 percent," said Andrew Pease, an economist at Nomura Research.
The last time unemployment hit 9.0 percent was in January 1995 when it was in a steadily declining trend having peaked at over 11.0 percent in 1993.

He also saw no early turnaround given the lagged effect of rate cuts on the economy, and the labour market in particular. "We do not expect a sustained recovery in employment growth until at least the end of the March quarter next year," he said.
The October jobs figures were just about strong enough to temper the clamouring in financial markets for another cut in official rates.

The 90-day bank bill future contract, which most closely reflects market thinking on policy, dipped six basis points to 93.77, although that still implied a rate of 6.33 percent against the current cash rate of 6.50 percent.

The Australian dollar softened to just below 79 cents from an early US$0.7915, but the dip was entirely due to a strong rise in the Japanese yen and dealers felt the data were modestly positive for the currency. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373-1800
